chapter_theme: Nedunalvadai describes the long cold season, first in the world and the town, then inside a king's palace, where the queen lies unadorned and unconsoled on a bed made for two; it ends with the poet's wish that the war end now, and with the king at midnight walking his winter camp to see his wounded, so that a poem the colophon files as vaakai spends most of its lines on a wife's waiting.
structure_note: The idyll is one sentence. Its ten units here follow its movements: the season outside (1-72), the palace and its inner chamber (73-114), the bed (115-135), the queen (136-166), and the prayer and the camp (167-188). All twelve core units were moved to sense breaks.

pattupattu:7:1-20.reading: When the unfailing clouds wheel to the right and pour new rain till the earth shivers, cowherds with crooked staffs drive their herds and bulls to other ground and, their kodal garlands sodden, shiver with firebrands held to their cheeks; beasts forget to graze, monkeys huddle, birds drop from their perches and cows kick away their calves; in the cold-season midnight that would chill a hill, musundai and gold-like peerkkai bloom on every bush, herons and storks pick fish on the wet white sand, and the emptied white clouds drift in drizzle across the sky.
pattupattu:7:1-20.nuance: The cold is shown entirely through what it does to bodies, the herders' chattering jaws, the monkeys' huddle, the birds that fall: a reader of the whole idyll will later meet a queen who shivers for another reason, but this unit names no lover at all.
pattupattu:7:1-20.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 1-16 and 17-32: the description of the first rains and of the creatures on the wet sand runs to line 20, where the spent clouds scatter drizzle; the fields and the town begin at line 21.

thinai_evidence.note: the cold season and midnight are kurinji's time (porul 1.7, 1.8), though no love situation is stated in the unit

comparisons.tenor: the cold of the season's midnight

pattupattu:7:21-35.reading: In the wide fields the paddy, grown thick in the rains, bows its coming ears; the clusters of the tall areca swell and their green nuts firm; the cold branches of the dense flowering groves drip; and in the rich old town of high mansions, along streets as broad as a river lying there, strong men in leaf garlands, drunk on bee-swarmed toddy, ignore the drizzle and wander past midday in cloth hanging on both sides as they please.
pattupattu:7:21-35.nuance: The men who ignore the rain are the only people in the season's prelude who enjoy it, and they enjoy it in company and drink; the contrast with the shut chambers to come is the poet's arrangement, not stated.
pattupattu:7:21-35.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 17-32 and 33-48: lines 21 to 35 move from the fields to the town and end with the drinkers wandering (திரிதர, line 35); the women of the evening begin at line 36.

thinai_evidence.note: watered fields, paddy and areca and a rich town are marutham things

comparisons.tenor: the dark green neck of the areca

pattupattu:7:36-48.reading: At evening young women with silver bangles on bamboo-smooth arms, soft gait, pearl smiles and cool eyes reaching to their flower earrings, knowing the hour by the scent of jasmine buds opening in their baskets, light the wet wicks of iron lamps, scatter paddy and flowers, join their hands and keep the evening rite in the rich market; while the red-legged male dove that lives in the house will not go out with his loving hen to feed in the common ground, but, unable to tell night from day, sits helpless on the rafter perch, shifting.
pattupattu:7:36-48.nuance: The dove that stays on the rafter with his mate in the cold is the first pair in the poem kept together by the season; it passes iraicchi's conditions 1 and 2 (one pair, an act) but the unit itself states no love situation for its sense to bear on, so it is left as scene.
pattupattu:7:36-48.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 33-48: it now begins at line 36, with the women who mark the evening, and ends at line 48 with the doves on the rafter.

thinai_evidence.note: evening is mullai's hour (porul 1.6), and the hour is known here by the opening of the jasmine

pattupattu:7:49-72.reading: In the guarded mansion the servants grind fragrant stone for many blends, the round stone the northerners brought lies unused with the southern sandal, the women wear no garlands and put only a few flowers in their dense hair, dried over fires of tagaram stems with dark aloe and white resin; spider webs hang on the folded fans; the summer chambers of the high upper storey that let in the south wind are shut with bolted doors; for the spray, no one drinks cold water from the jars but all sit by the braziers; the dancing women warm against their breasts the lute strings gone slack in the cold before they tune the small lute; and so, while the rains thicken and those parted from their lovers lament, the cold season has set in.
pattupattu:7:49-72.nuance: Twenty-two lines of a household's defences against the cold (fires, shut doors, no cold water, warmed strings) end in a single clause naming the people the season hurts, the parted lovers; the line's formula is shared with Akananuru 264, where பொழுதே stands for this போதே. The sense of கொள்ளுறழ் நறுங்கல் in line 50 is not secure.
pattupattu:7:49-72.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 49-64 and 65-80: the season's description is one sentence that closes at line 72 with கூதிர்நின் றன்றாற் போதே; the palace building begins with மாதிரம் at the end of that line, which is kept with this unit.

thinai_evidence.note: the only love situation in the unit is the lament of those whose lovers are away, the waiting of mullai

pattupattu:7:73-100.reading: At midday, when the spreading sun throws no slant from the two marker poles, builders who know the treatise stretch their cord, take the directions, worship the gods and lay out a house fit for great kings; inside its high encircling wall stands a gateway tall as a cut hill, with paired doors bound in iron, posts of a fine tree named for a star, a lintel carved with a newly opened water-lily, smeared with white mustard and ghee, high enough for an elephant with its victory flag to pass; in the courtyard of spread sand male swans with long feathers play with short-legged hens, maned horses tired of the stall chew their grass with lonely cries, rain-water pours from the gaping makara spouts, and peacocks call like horns from a palace that rings like a mountain slope.
pattupattu:7:73-100.nuance: The courtyard's swans play in pairs and its horse cries alone (புலம்புவிடு குரல்), so even the description of masonry carries the poem's two states, together and parted.
pattupattu:7:73-100.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 65-80, 81-96 and 97-112: the building of the palace runs from மாதிரம் at the end of line 72 (kept with the previous unit) to கோயில், line 100, where the sentence on the outer palace ends.

thinai_evidence.note: the unit praises the excellence of the builders and the king's house; no love situation is stated

pattupattu:7:101-114.reading: In the palace, lamp-figures made by Yavanas hold bowls brimming with ghee whose thick wicks raise upright flames, trimmed whenever they burn low, so that the spreading dark leaves every chamber; within the hard-guarded precinct that no man but the great lord may approach stand rooms like hills, creepers like bows, walls plastered bright as silver, pillars dark and thick as gems, walls red as wrought copper painted round with a single creeper of many flowers, and among them the fine chamber named for the womb.
pattupattu:7:101-114.nuance: That only the great lord (பெருந்தகை) may enter the precinct makes the chamber's emptiness the king's absence; the unit is architecture, but it locks the door that the poem will not open again.
pattupattu:7:101-114.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 97-112 and 113-128: the inner palace is one description from the Yavana lamps (line 101) to the chamber named for the womb (கருவொடு பெயரிய காண்பி னல்லில், line 114); the couch begins at line 115.

thinai_evidence.note: craft and splendour of the king's inner palace, with no love situation stated

pattupattu:7:115-135.reading: In that chamber stands a full-sized couch on strong legs, swelling like drums, cut from the tusks of a forty-year elephant fallen in battle and shaped with a sharp chisel by a master, the legs rounded like the breasts of women heavy with child and narrowing at the middle, set on garlic-shaped feet; it is strung with fine work and hung with a lattice of pearls, its board covered with a tiger-spotted spread whose dyed cushions picture a hunt of strong beasts in a wide forest among flowers set like mullai buds; on it a soft bed, paired pillows filled with the white down of swans that had mated, and a washed, starched white sheet over all.
pattupattu:7:115-135.nuance: The down is from swans that had mated (துணைபுணர்) and the pillows are a pair (இணையணை): the bed is made for two in every detail before the next unit lays one woman on it. Lines 115 to 117, on the elephant's age and how its tusk was taken, are hard to construe.
pattupattu:7:115-135.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 113-128 and 129-144: the couch and bedding are one description from line 115 to the spread sheet (சேக்கை, line 135); the queen on it begins at line 136.

thinai_evidence.note: the bed is described for the absent pair, and its patterned flowers are likened to mullai

comparisons.tenor: the flowers set on the spread

pattupattu:7:136-156.reading: On it lies the queen: on her breast, where the necklace lay, only a long plait hangs; her few soft locks lie dry over her fair brow; her ears, the long earrings removed, keep only small rings; her wrists, bared of gold bangles, carry only the right-whorled conch bangle and a protective thread, her finger a red ring bent like a vaalai fish's mouth, and her waist a soiled cloth, so that she looks like a picture left uncoloured; soft-limbed maids rub her feet, and grey-haired, red-faced foster mothers crowd round her, telling tales short and long and saying her dear one will come at once, all to please her; but she will not take comfort and weeps.
pattupattu:7:136-156.nuance: Each ornament is named with the token kept in its place (the plait for the necklace, the small ring for the earring, the conch bangle and thread for the gold), so a wife's karpu is read off what she has given up. The nurses' இன்னே வருகுவர் is the same promise Mullaippattu's old women hear in an omen; here it is only talk, and it fails. The colophon gives no speaker; the nurses' words are the unit's own speech.
pattupattu:7:136-156.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 129-144, 145-155 and 156-171: the queen and the nurses' comfort form one sentence that closes with ஒல்லாள் மிகக்கலுழ்ந்து in line 156; line 156 is kept here and the painted canopy begins at line 157.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife waiting through the season for the husband away at war, comforted with the promise of his return

pattupattu:7:157-166.reading: She looks up at the canopy newly painted in wax on cloth over strong round posts, where the ram heads the circle of signs travelling the sky and the moon, the glorious lord, is shown with Rohini who never leaves him; thinking of Rohini she sighs long, gathers with her red finger-tips the tears that fall from the corners of her dark-lidded eyes and flicks a few away, and lies alone with her grief, this woman of shining beauty.
pattupattu:7:157-166.nuance: The poem says only that she thinks of Rohini and sighs; the contrast with the star that stays with her lord is left for the reader. It is not tagged ullurai or iraicchi, since the vehicle is a painted star and not a native thing of the land (porul 1.50). Lines 157 and 158, on how the canopy posts are made, are obscure.
pattupattu:7:157-166.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 156-171: the canopy, the sigh and the tears are one clause that ends with புலம்பொடு வதியு நலங்கிளர் அரிவைக்கு, line 166; the poet's prayer for her begins at line 167.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife lies alone in grief waiting for the absent husband

comparisons.tenor: the knobs of the canopy posts

pattupattu:7:167-188.reading: May the war end now with victory, the poet prays, so that this bright woman's hard grief may end; for at the deep midnight the king, not taking to his bed, walks with a few men about the camp that is at war with many, going out to see the bright sword wounds of the warriors who brought down elephants whose long trunks now roll on the ground; the flames of the many lamps lean south as the cold north wind strikes them, a leader shows the wounded one by one with a strong neem-tied spear, harnessed horses shake off the rain in the muddy lane, and with his left hand holding his slipping cloth and his other arm on the shoulder of a sword-bearing youth, he looks at each face kindly while a pearl-strung white umbrella keeps off the falling drops.
pattupattu:7:167-188.nuance: The whole idyll is one sentence that ends on பாசறைத் தொழிலே, and the king is never named: the neem on the spear is the only sign that he is the Pandya, and the poet's wish in lines 167 and 168 is the only bridge between the queen's chamber and the camp, which never meet in the poem.
pattupattu:7:167-188.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 156-171 and 172-188: the poet's wish (இன்னே முடிகதில், lines 167, 168) is the main clause on which the closing camp scene depends, so the unit runs from line 167 to the end of the poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's work in the winter camp and the warriors' wounds, framed by the wish that the queen's grief end

links.note: Both open the cold season with white musundai, kodal and cowherds coming in from the rain with wet garlands, and both close the description with the same words, கூதிர்நின் றன்றால் followed by பொழுதே (here போதே, line 72).
links.teaches: In Akananuru 264 the formula hands the season to a waiting woman who asks whether the men in the king's camp know their own state, so the idyll's cold-season opening, which ends on the same words, reads as that akam season-poem expanded, with its closing camp scene as the answer to her question.

links.note: In both idylls the waiting wife is told இன்னே வருகுவர் and still weeps; in Mullaippattu the words are an omen overheard from a herd girl to her calves, in Nedunalvadai they are the foster mothers' practised comfort.
links.teaches: Mullaippattu's promise is a sign that its poem fulfils with the returning chariot, while Nedunalvadai's is only kind speech that its poem never fulfils, so the same words separate a poem of waiting rewarded from one that can end only in the poet's wish.

links.note: The queen gazes at a painted moon with Rohini and sighs; Akananuru 136 sets a wedding at the hour when the moon had joined Sakatam, the Rohini asterism, in a spotless conjunction.
links.teaches: Since weddings were timed to the moon's union with Rohini, the painting over the queen's bed is also the sign under which she was married, so her long sigh can be read as memory of her own wedding as well as envy of a pair never parted.

links.note: The Kural counts every day without a glorious wound (விழுப்புண்) as wasted; the idyll's king walks the camp at midnight in the rain to see the glorious wounds (விழுப்புண்) of the warriors who felled elephants.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the wound a soldier's private reckoning of his days, and the idyll shows its public side, the king coming out at night to look at each wound, so the honour the soldier counts by was conferred in person by his king's seeing it.

links.note: In both a king in a rain-soaked camp will not sleep (கண்படை இலனே; பள்ளி கொள்ளான்); in Akananuru the soldier cites it to tell his heart the war is his duty while she hears the evening alone, in Nedunalvadai the poet sets it beside the queen's grief and prays for the war's end.
links.teaches: The king's sleepless diligence is the soldier's reason for staying away in the Akananuru and the poet's ground for hoping the war ends soon in the idyll, so one camp image can either lengthen the separation or promise its end, depending on whose grief frames it.

links.note: Mullaippattu's king lies sleepless in his tent thinking of elephants wounded by spears and of men who fell repaying their food; Nedunalvadai's king rises and goes out at midnight to see his wounded.
links.teaches: The two camp kings show one care in two forms, remembered in bed in Mullaippattu and acted out by walking the lines in Nedunalvadai, so the night-time thought for the wounded is a fixed mark of the good war king in these idylls, the more vivid of them putting it into motion.

links.note: Yavanas make the lamp-figures that light the queen's inner chambers in Nedunalvadai; in Mullaippattu fierce armed Yavanas guard the king's tent.
links.teaches: Read together, the idylls place Yavanas at both ends of a royal household, as craftsmen inside the women's palace and as bodyguards in the war camp, so the king trusted these foreigners with the light of his queen's rooms and with his own person.

new_concepts.gloss: the cold season after the rains, of north wind and drizzle; in the Tholkappiyam the season of kurinji
new_concepts.label_source: text: கூதிர்ப் பானாள் line 12, கூதிர்நின் றன்றாற் line 72, and the colophon thurai கூதிர்ப்பாசறை

new_concepts.gloss: the war camp of a king in the field, where the army stays through a campaign
new_concepts.label_source: text: பாசறைத் தொழிலே line 188, and the colophon thurai

source_issues: Line 17 நாரைய டெவ்வாயுங் is நாரையொடு எவ்வாயும் with the vowel sign ொ lost, the same loss show flags at lines 46, 82, 84, 142, 169 and 178 but not flagged here; the karu form is copied as printed.
Line 35 இருகோட்ட டறுவையர் has a doubled ட (expected இருகோட் டறுவையர், two-ended cloth); probably a typing error.
Line 110 விளங்குஞ் கதையுரீஇ: ஞ் before க is not regular sandhi, and கதை makes no sense here; the expected reading is விளங்கும் சுதையுரீஇ (plastered with lime). The reading follows சுதை.
Line 72 has போதே where the same formula in Akananuru 264 line 10 has பொழுதே; both are read as the season (time) having set in.
The colophon gives no patron, though the neem tied to the spear (வேம்புதலை, line 176) marks the king as a Pandya; the poem names no one.
